newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Prisoner issue seems blocking Afghan rivals talks.
newsitem.headline: Prisoner issue seems blocking Afghan rivals talks.

text.p: The Taleban Islamic movement and Afghanistan's main northern opposition leader both said on Sunday they wanted to hold talks but Taleban's precondition for the release of prisoners appeared a stumbling block.

Taleban spokesman Wakil Ahmed said by telephone from the southern town of Kandahar that his fundamentalist Islamic militia was prepared for peace talks with the northern opposition leader General Abdul Malik.
But he added: "Release of prisoners held by them (opposition forces) ... is a precondition for talks."

Several Taleban officials, including former foreign minister Mullah Mohammad Ghous, and an unspecified number of fighters were arrested by Malik's forces late last month when he turned against the Taleban after a short-lived alliance and drove them from Mazar-i-Sharif.
Malik, apparently side-stepping the prisoner issue, told reporters his forces were ready for talks with the Taleban on holding free elections in the war-shattered country.
Ahmed did not rule out the possibility of the Taleban, which controls more than two-third of Afghanistan and the capital Kabul, reaching an understanding with opposition forces controlling the north.
The opposition says it is holding several thousand prisoners, and Malik said they included 400 Pakistanis.
Pakistan says none of its nationals are fighting in Afghanistan.
Taleban forces have suffered a string of reverses north of Kabul since they were forced to retreat from the newly captured Mazar-i-Sharif.

A Pakistan-based Aghan news service on Sunday reported that Taleban forces had retreated on Saturday from Asmar in the eastern province of Kunar, which borders Pakistan, after clashes with local opposition.
It was not clear whether Taleban opponents had taken control of Asmar.
Military and opposition sources in Mazar-i-Sharif said on Saturday opposition forces had advanced to within a few km (miles) of the Taleban-held Bagram airbase north of Kabul.

A military source said guerrillas loyal to former government commander Ahmad Shah Masood had launched an offensive on Thursday, driving the Taleban out of the town of Jabal-os-Siraj, 70 km (44 miles) north of Kabul.
They were now fighting for the Soviet-built Bagram airbase, 50 km (30 miles) from the capital.
The source said the Taleban had repulsed an assault on Bagram on Friday, but some fighting was continuing. He had no immediate word on casualties on either side.
